body.text: Carryback of ITC lets Canadian taxpayers claiming SR&ED investment tax credits apply unused, unrefunded current-year credits against federal Part I tax payable in up to 3 preceding taxation years, limited to that year's tax not already offset by ITCs. Unused credits can be carried forward 20 years, and any ITC carried back reduces the following year's Section 37 pool.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program represents the country’s single largest federal source of support for business-led research and development, supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually according to practitioner estimates. Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA, which oversees technical and financial compliance, administration, and audit reviews), the program operates through a dual-mechanism architecture embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (the "ITA" or "the Act") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (the "Regulations" or "ITR"). First, Subsection 37(1) of the ITA enables taxpayers to pool allowable current and qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures for immediate deduction against business income or indefinite carryforward to future taxation years. Second, Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA provide an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated on "qualified expenditures," yielding either cash refunds, reductions of Part I federal tax payable, or both, with unused non-refunded credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward.

As of 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape has undergone its most consequential legislative transformation since the 2012–2014 reforms. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, enacting major enhancements initially proposed in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement and expanded in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and applying to depreciable capital property acquired or equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable federal ITC from $3 million to $6 million (raising the maximum annual cash refund to $2.1 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a 3-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), allowed CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out regime, and restored SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322), while at the provincial level, Québec enacted the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 (consolidating legacy R&D measures into a unified 30%/20% refundable credit covering R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital equipment), British Columbia made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent effective April 16, 2026, and Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable expenditure cap to $2 million.
1. Statutory and Legislative Framework
1.1 Dual-Pillar Statutory Architecture in the Income Tax Act

The Canadian federal SR&ED tax incentive regime is codified across three primary divisions of the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. Subsection 248(1) of the ITA serves as the definitional gatekeeper, establishing the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (SR&ED) alongside core foundational terms such as "salary or wages" and "specified employee". Unless an activity satisfies the technical definition in Subsection 248(1)—encompassing basic research under paragraph (a), applied research under paragraph (b), experimental development under paragraph (c), and eligible support work under paragraph (d), while avoiding the seven statutory exclusions under paragraphs (e) through (k)—no expenditure associated with that activity can enter the SR&ED tax calculation.

Once technical eligibility under Subsection 248(1) is established, Section 37 of the ITA governs the computation of the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada (Subsection 37(1)) and permissible research conducted outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2)). Section 37 allows a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to accumulate allowable current expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(a)) and qualifying capital expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b), restored for property acquired after December 15, 2024) in a perpetual tax pool. Taxpayers may deduct all or any portion of the positive year-end balance of the Section 37 pool when computing net income for tax purposes for the current taxation year, carrying forward any undeducted balance indefinitely to future taxation years, subject to loss restriction event (acquisition-of-control) limitations under Subsection 37(6.1).

In parallel with the Section 37 deduction pool, Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA govern the conversion of "qualified expenditures" (defined in Subsection 127(9)) and the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" into federal Investment Tax Credits. Subsection 127(5) governs the deduction of ITCs against Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, while Subsection 127(10.1) and Section 127.1 govern the 20% ITC enhancement (creating the 35% enhanced rate) and the refundability of unused ITCs for qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, individuals, and trusts. Operational rules linking Section 37 and Section 127 are codified in Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900–2903), which prescribe the tests for directly attributable expenditures under the Traditional Method (Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on the direct SR&ED salary base under the Proxy Method (Subsection 2900(4)), specified employee proxy salary base limits (Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(9)), Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) rules (Subsection 2900(11)), Prescribed Expenditures excluded from earning ITCs (Section 2902), and special-purpose buildings (Section 2903).

body.text: 1.2 The 2025–2026 Legislative Overhaul: Bill C-15 and Budget 2025 Enactment

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the federal SR&ED legislative framework progressed through three major legislative stages. First, in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled on December 16, 2024), the Department of Finance proposed modernizing the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, initially proposing to raise the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, widen the CCPC prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extend the enhanced 35% credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restore capital expenditure and equipment lease cost eligibility.

Second, on August 15, 2025, the Department of Finance released detailed draft legislative proposals for public consultation (which closed September 12, 2025), followed on November 4, 2025, by the presentation of the 2025 Federal Budget by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne. Budget 2025 further increased the enhanced annual expenditure limit from the previously proposed $4.5 million to $6 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

Third, on March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, formally enacting the $6 million expenditure limit, the $15 million–$75 million phase-out thresholds, ECPC eligibility, CCPC gross revenue election optionality, and the restoration of capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs into the Income Tax Act. Following Royal Assent, the CRA issued updated prescribed forms—including revised Form T661 on May 15, 2026, Form T1145 and Form T1146 on May 15, 2026, Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026, and Schedule T2SCH49 on May 29, 2026—and published updated administrative policies between May and October 2026.
2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria
2.1 The Statutory Definition: Subsection 248(1) Inclusions and Exclusions

Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition bifurcates eligible activities into three core categories of direct R&D work and one category of derivative support work, while imposing seven absolute exclusions.
A. The Three Core Categories of SR&ED (Paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), and (c))

Paragraph 248(1)(a) defines basic research as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research seeks to expand the underlying base of theoretical or empirical scientific knowledge—such as characterizing the properties of elementary particles like the electron or studying a newly discovered virus to understand its biological characteristics—and is typically conducted in laboratory environments, with findings frequently published in scientific journals.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) defines applied research as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. While sharing the same scientific methodology and knowledge-generation objective as basic research, applied research is directed toward a defined commercial or practical objective—such as investigating how electron conductivity in semiconductor materials can be controlled to create a solid-state amplifier, or developing a vaccine against a newly discovered virus by exploiting its identified characteristics.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) defines experimental development as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Accounting for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada, experimental development does not require advancing pure scientific knowledge; rather, it advances technology (the practical application of scientific knowledge and engineering principles) by resolving technological uncertainties encountered when developing working prototypes, scaling up and optimizing vaccine or industrial manufacturing processes, or re-architecting complex systems.
B. Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d))

Work that does not independently constitute basic research, applied research, or experimental development qualifies as SR&ED under Paragraph 248(1)(d) only if it is undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to one of eight exhaustive statutory categories—namely engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. "Commensurate with the needs" requires that the amount, size, extent, and duration of the support work correspond strictly to what is needed to carry out the underlying SR&ED investigation; any excess work beyond what is required for the SR&ED is excluded.

Crucially, support work is never eligible on its own. In software development claims, for example, "computer programming" is enumerated in Paragraph 248(1)(d) as a category of support work. Consequently, coding standard CRUD features, user dashboards, or payment integrations is outside SR&ED; computer programming qualifies only when it directly supports and is proportionate to resolving an underlying technological uncertainty in experimental development, such as developing a novel real-time anomaly detection algorithm where published methods cannot meet latency constraints. Similarly, an arm's-length contractor hired solely to perform support work cannot claim SR&ED tax incentives on its own tax return (because support work alone does not meet the definition of SR&ED), whereas the contracting payer can claim the contract expenditure if the contractor's support work is directly in support of and commensurate with the needs of basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed by or on behalf of the payer.
C. The Seven Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-technological work from the definition of SR&ED, none of which can be claimed:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives explain, the decisive factor distinguishing eligible support work under Paragraph (d) (such as "data collection" or "testing") from excluded work under Paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is purpose. Work carried out as a routine activity to support normal commercial operations—such as data collection or testing for quality control or routine quality assurance—is excluded under Paragraphs (f) and (k). Conversely, if data collection or testing is carried out specifically to directly support basic research, applied research, or experimental development (for example, testing a newly scaled-up vaccine production process to evaluate experimental parameters), it qualifies as eligible support work under Paragraph (d).
2.2 The CRA "Why" and "How" Administrative Framework (2021/2022 Guidelines)

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA replaced its archived 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the statutory definition in Subsection 248(1) remained unchanged, the CRA structured its administrative evaluation around two mandatory requirements that must both be met.

First, under The "Why" Requirement, the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The objective must be generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories, principles, or prediction models) rather than merely factual knowledge (such as data or measurements gathered via known techniques). New conceptual knowledge is needed only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—meaning it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in available scientific or technological knowledge (considering both the internal knowledge of the business and publicly available sources). The CRA identifies seven specific characteristics indicating that available technological knowledge is insufficient: existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; too many variables or unknowns exist; parameters or conditions fall outside the normal operating range; the nature of the problem is evolving; data is not readily available; or interlocking constraints exist (including technological uncertainty imposed by economic considerations when trying to meet reasonable cost targets). Circumventing an uncertainty via a workaround using existing available knowledge, or acquiring available knowledge through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge, does not meet the "Why" requirement. Conversely, failing to achieve the targeted objective does not disqualify the work, provided the purpose was to advance scientific or technological knowledge by attempting to resolve the uncertainty.

Second, under The "How" Requirement, the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Following standard procedures or adopting a systematic business approach alone is insufficient; a systematic investigation or search requires four operational elements: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the problem; (2) testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing); (3) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (4) keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses.
2.3 The Binding Judicial Standard: The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Test

Notwithstanding administrative guidelines published by the CRA, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) have repeatedly affirmed that the binding legal test for SR&ED eligibility in Canada is the Five-Question Test formulated by Justice Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520 (TCC), and formally confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 CTC 132 (FCA), C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72. In National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) and Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2023 TCC 35), the courts explicitly rejected taxpayer arguments that the CRA's 2021 Guidelines removed the requirement to follow the scientific method. To qualify for SR&ED, a claimant must establish that each of the five questions is answered in the affirmative (Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205):

items: Question 1 — Scientific or Technological Uncertainty: Was there a scientific or technological uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Technical risk or uncertainty must be incapable of resolution through "routine engineering," which refers to techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. If competent specialists can resolve the problem in a reasonably predictable way using established techniques, there is no technological uncertainty—even if the required knowledge was unknown to the claimant itself or if there was doubt regarding how the commercial objective would be achieved.

Question 2 — Formulation of Hypotheses: Were hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty formulated? Justice Bowman established that this criterion involves a five-step process: (1) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (2) formulation of a clear objective; (3) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (4) formulation of a hypothesis designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (5) methodical and systematic testing of the hypothesis or hypotheses. Identifying new technological uncertainties as the research progresses is an integral part of this scientific method.

Question 3 — Systematic Investigation and Scientific Method: Was the overall procedure adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including the formulation and testing of hypotheses through experiments or analysis? While intuitive creativity and genius may play a crucial role, they must operate within the total discipline of the scientific method. Furthermore, what may appear routine and obvious after the event may not have been routine or obvious before the work was undertaken.

Question 4 — Scientific or Technological Advancement: Was the overall approach adopted aimed at achieving a scientific or technological advancement? Advancement refers to an advancement in general understanding available to persons knowledgeable in the field. The rejection of a hypothesis after testing still constitutes an advancement because it eliminates a previously untested hypothesis, and failure may reinforce the measure of the technological uncertainty.

Question 5 — Contemporaneous Detailed Records: Was a detailed record or report of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed? Keeping a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses is implicit within the notion of the "scientific method" and the statutory requirement for a "systematic investigation" under Subsection 248(1) of the Act.

body.text: 3. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Outs, and Carryforwards
3.1 Dual-Tier Federal Investment Tax Credit Structure (Section 127 & Section 127.1)

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates across two statutory rate tiers under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. The Basic ITC Rate of 15% is earned on qualified SR&ED expenditures by corporations (including non-CCPC/non-ECPC large or foreign-controlled corporations, as well as CCPCs and ECPCs on qualified expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietorships), members of a partnership, and beneficiaries of a trust. The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35%—which equals the 15% basic rate plus an additional 20% enhancement rate under Subsection 127(10.1)—is earned on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate applied exclusively to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3 million. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 increased the maximum annual expenditure limit to $6 million and expanded access to the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).
3.2 Corporate Classifications: Qualifying CCPCs, Excluded Corporations, and ECPCs
The applicable ITC rate and cash refundability percentage depend on four statutory corporate classifications defined in Subsections 125(7), 127(9), and 127.1(2) of the ITA:

items: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC — Subsection 125(7)): A private corporation that is a Canadian corporation not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, one or more public corporations, or a combination thereof.

Qualifying Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)): A CCPC whose taxable income (combined with all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year) does not exceed the corporation's "qualifying income limit" for the year.
Excluded Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)): A CCPC that is controlled by, or related to, one or more persons exempt from Part I tax under Section 149.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC — Subsection 127(9)): For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a corporation qualifies as an ECPC if, throughout the taxation year, it (1) is a resident of Canada, (2) has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or has elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation), and (3) is not controlled, directly or indirectly, by one or more non-resident persons. Canadian-resident corporations substantially owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible under the ECPC rules.

body.text: 3.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue
A. Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out for CCPCs (Subsection 127(10.2))

For a CCPC (and its associated group of CCPCs), the annual expenditure limit decreases based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) for the previous taxation year. Associated CCPCs must allocate the shared expenditure limit using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit).

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $10,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) at $50,000,000:
Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (enacted under Bill C-15), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit of a CCPC begins to decrease when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000:
Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000
B. Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out for ECPCs and Electing CCPCs

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—and for CCPCs that elect by prescribed form to use the gross revenue structure instead of the taxable capital structure—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis when average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (and is fully eliminated at $75,000,000):

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if 3-year average annual gross revenue is $15,000,000 or less, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of 3-year average annual gross revenue over $15,000,000. For ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group preparing consolidated financial statements, the expenditure limit is shared among the group members, and the annual revenue reflected in the group's consolidated financial statements is used to calculate the 3-year average annual revenue. For associated CCPCs electing the revenue structure, the calculation aggregates the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of all associated group members over the preceding 3 fiscal years regardless of whether they were associated throughout that entire period. Where a corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 365 days), its allocated expenditure limit is prorated under Subsection 127(10.5) by the number of days in the short tax year divided by 365.
3.4 Refundability Matrix and Carryover Rules

Under Section 127.1 of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), cash refundability of unused current-year ITCs depends on corporate status, whether the expenditures are within or above the expenditure limit, and whether the expenditures are current (including the PPA) or capital.

body.text: Under Subsection 127(5) and Subsection 127.1(3) (Deemed Deduction), a taxpayer may apply available current-year ITCs to reduce Part I federal tax otherwise payable to nil, and any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been applied against Part I tax, thereby reducing the ITC balance available for carryback or carryforward. Unapplied, unrefunded current-year ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the excess of Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year over ITCs already available in that prior year) and carried forward for up to 20 taxation years. Any SR&ED ITC utilized in a taxation year (whether refunded in cash, applied against current Part I tax, or carried back) reduces the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year; if this deduction drives the Section 37 pool negative at year-end, the negative balance must be included in taxable income under Paragraph 12(1)(v) (and is added back to the Section 37 pool in the subsequent year under Paragraph 37(1)(c.1)). Finally, an acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of pre-acquisition Section 37 pool balances (Subsection 37(6.1)) and pre-acquisition ITCs, as well as the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
4.1 The Two-Step Calculation: Section 37 Pool vs. Section 127 Qualified Expenditures

Calculating a Canadian SR&ED claim requires executing two related but distinct statutory calculations on Form T661. First, in Part 3 of Form T661, the claimant selects either the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method on Line 160, identifies total allowable current expenditures (Line 380) and capital expenditures (Line 390) to arrive at Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures on Line 400, and adjusts for assistance, prior-year ITCs used, and recaptures to determine the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Second, in Part 4 and Part 5 of Form T661, starting with Line 400, the claimant adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (if using the Proxy Method) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504: 25% of capital cost for first-term and second-term SUE), and deducts 20% of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, non-arm's length contracts, prescribed expenditures (such as used capital property on Line 535), unpaid non-wage current amounts under the 180-day rule, and government/non-government assistance to arrive at Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Section 127 ITC Purposes.
4.2 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method Election (Subsection 37(8))

A claimant must select either the Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) on a year-by-year basis on Line 160 of Form T661. Once Form T661 is filed for a particular taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that taxation year and cannot be changed, although the claimant is free to choose either method in subsequent taxation years. If a claimant does not explicitly elect to use the Proxy Method on Line 160 when filing its first Form T661 for the year, the Traditional Method applies automatically by default.

body.text: 4.3 Salaries and Wages (ITA Subsections 37(8), 37(9.1), 78(4) & Salary or Wages Policy)

Under Subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I (generally T4 employment income), excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances.
A. Inclusions, Exclusions, Directly Engaged Criteria, Unpaid Wages, and Foreign Work

Allowable SR&ED salaries and wages include regular salaries/wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, regular sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, gratuities, honoraria, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducement/non-competition payments, bonuses and remuneration based on profits (for employees other than specified employees), and taxable benefits (where paid in cash, or non-cash benefits where the value is a reasonable estimate of actual cost excluding GST/HST/PST for which an input tax credit is claimed and the underlying cost is not also deducted as a business expense). Conversely, SR&ED salaries and wages strictly exclude dividends (which are distributions of profit, not employment income), stock option benefits (deemed not to be an expenditure incurred), the employer's share of related payroll benefits (such as CPP, EI, or group insurance, which are covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method or claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), extended vacation or extended sick leave, and retiring allowances.

Under the Proxy Method, only the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED in Canada (determined by actual tasks performed rather than job title, including direct technical supervision by an employee with a significant technological background) may be claimed. Under the Traditional Method, salaries of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED are eligible (and where all or substantially all [ASA — 90% or more] of an employee's time is devoted to SR&ED, 100% of their salary is eligible), while administrative salaries must satisfy the "directly related and incremental" tests and are restricted to the actual percentage of time spent.

Under Subsection 78(4) of the ITA, employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (and is excluded from the PPA salary base in that subsequent year under Regulation 2900(9)). Furthermore, under Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees may be claimed up to a maximum of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada, provided the foreign work is performed solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada and the remuneration is not subject to an income or profits tax from another country. Permissible foreign SR&ED wages are excluded from the Proxy Method PPA salary base, and no foreign overhead or travel expenses are deductible under Subsection 37(1).
B. Specified Employees: Dual Caps (5× YMPE vs. 2.5× YMPE / 75%) and Bonus Disallowance

A "specified employee" is defined in Subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, including shares owned by non-arm's length persons) or who does not deal at arm's length with a specified shareholder (such as a spouse, sibling, or child). Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions:

items: Disallowance of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: All bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are 100% excluded from allowable SR&ED salaries and wages.

Total Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap — 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): Under Subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated by the number of days in the tax year on which the individual is a specified employee: Maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages = 5 × YMPE × (number of days in the tax year on which the individual is a specified employee ÷ 365).

body.text: If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the 5 × YMPE cap must be allocated among them using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)), accompanied by a certified copy of the Directors' resolution authorizing the allocation; otherwise, no amount may be claimed. 3. Proxy Method Salary Base Cap — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulations 2900(7) & 2900(9)): For the purpose of calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method, Regulation 2900(9) excludes taxable benefits, prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year, bonuses, and profit-based remuneration, and Regulation 2900(7) restricts the specified employee's inclusion in the PPA Salary Base to the lesser of: (i) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages), or (ii) 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the tax year (shared across associated corporations):

body.text: 4.4 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Overall Cap Formula (Regulation 2900(4)–(10))

Under Subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026), claimants electing the Proxy Method calculate the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. The PPA is a notional amount included solely in qualified expenditures for Section 127 ITC purposes; it is not added to the Section 37 deduction pool, as the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA are deducted as ordinary business expenses.
Furthermore, Regulation 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA to ensure that the PPA does not exceed the claimant's actual non-SR&ED business deductions for the year, calculated by the formula:

Overall PPA Cap = A − (B + C), where A is the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold); B is the total deductions claimed in the year under Sections 20 (CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED pool deductions), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts) of the ITA; and C is the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building.
4.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and Paragraph 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method) and Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), a claimant may claim the laid-down cost (acquisition invoice cost, customs/excise duties, transportation, and storage, or industrial production cost including raw materials, direct labour, and allocated production overhead for internally manufactured inventory) of materials either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

According to the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), to qualify as "materials for SR&ED," the items must be physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible thing on which the SR&ED is being carried out, or a tangible object resulting from the SR&ED. Consequently, laboratory supplies and utilities that do not compose the body of the object under investigation—such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, test tubes, filter papers, microscopes, cleaning supplies, acids/solvents/lubricants used in processing, CDs/DVDs, and general utilities (electricity, water, gas)—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED (though they may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), nor do capital/enduring expenditures such as equipment, datasets, or software licences. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year they are actually consumed or transformed (and must be paid within 180 days of year-end under Subsection 127(26)), and purchases from non-arm's length suppliers are restricted for ITC purposes to the supplier's cost excluding profit under Subsection 127(11.6).

Materials Consumed are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED. If experimental production is sold for more than 10% of its original cost, the materials are considered not to have been consumed, and instead constitute Materials Transformed (materials changed or incorporated into another product, custom product, or commercial asset that retains value). If a product, prototype, or asset containing transformed materials is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the ITC Recapture Rules under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) apply to claw back the ITC previously claimed.
4.6 Overhead and Other Expenditures — Traditional Method Tests & Cloud Computing Costs

Under Paragraph 2900(2)(c) and Subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), overhead and other current expenditures can only be claimed under the Traditional Method on Line 360 of Form T661, and must satisfy two mandatory tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect directly—without any intervening step or intermediary—to one of three elements: (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred.

body.text: In software and AI claims, cloud computing costs (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform) and third-party APIs must first be strictly segregated between commercial "production infrastructure" (Cost of Goods Sold, which is ineligible) and isolated "development/R&D infrastructure" tagged to SR&ED projects. Because cloud compute and software subscriptions are not physical tangible objects, they cannot be claimed as "materials". Under the Proxy Method, cloud hosting and software costs are covered by the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately; under the Traditional Method, incremental R&D cloud costs directly linked to SR&ED experimentation can be claimed on Line 360 as overhead. Additionally, physical GPU clusters and compute servers acquired or leased after December 15, 2024, qualify under the restored capital expenditure and equipment lease rules.

Even if directly related and incremental under the Traditional Method, Paragraph 2902(a) of the Regulations excludes Prescribed Expenditures from earning ITCs, including: third-party SR&ED claim preparation fees (financial or technical consulting/accounting fees, whereas salaries of the claimant's own regular employees preparing the claim remain eligible under Clause 2902(a)(i)(B)), legal and accounting fees, interest and financing costs (Paragraphs 20(1)(c)–(g)), entertainment, advertising/selling expenses, conference/convention expenses, scientific society membership dues, and fines/penalties. Similarly, headhunter fees, job advertising, and work permit/immigration fees for hiring SR&ED staff are excluded, whereas moving expenses to relocate selected SR&ED candidates or employees within Canada qualify under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental.
4.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Effective for depreciable property acquired and becoming available for use after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs first becoming payable/incurred after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored SR&ED eligibility for capital equipment, SUE, and leased equipment.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Line 390 of Form T661 & ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire new or used depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 once the property becomes available for use (under Subsections 37(1.2) and 13(27)) if the claimant intends that the property will either: (1) be used all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (2) have all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its value consumed to perform SR&ED in Canada. Both new and used ASA depreciable property enter the Section 37 deduction pool on Line 390; however, under Paragraph 2902(b) of the Regulations, used property is a prescribed capital expenditure that must be deducted on Line 535 in Part 4 of Form T661 and does not earn an SR&ED ITC (unless refurbished by a vendor so extensively prior to acquisition as to be considered "new," or to the extent of subsequent refurbishment costs incurred by the claimant). Land (non-depreciable), buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, and property used outside Canada are excluded, as is General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) under the Proxy Method. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC on new ASA capital property up to their $6 million expenditure limit, the cash refund rate on capital ITCs is 40%. Claimants report up to the 10 most expensive ASA capital properties per project on Lines 262 and 263 of Part 2, and up to the 20 most expensive capital properties across all projects in Part 6B (Boxes 780, 782, 786) of Form T661.
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504 of Form T661 & ITA Subsection 127(9))

Under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test (and is neither GPOEF nor Prescribed Depreciable Property under Regulation 2900(11)) qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time, up to <90%) for SR&ED in Canada. The capital cost of SUE is not included in the Section 37 deduction pool (and is instead depreciated via regular Capital Cost Allowance on Schedule T2SCH8). For Section 127 ITC purposes (calculated identically under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods), the claimant claims 25% (1/4) of the capital cost on Line 504 as First-Term SUE if the equipment is used >50% for SR&ED in the First Period (starting on the acquisition/available-for-use date and ending at the end of the first tax year ending at least 12 months later), and an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost on Line 504 as Second-Term SUE if it continues to be used >50% for SR&ED in the Second Period (starting on the acquisition date and ending at the end of the first tax year ending at least 24 months later)—for a cumulative maximum of 50% of capital cost. Up to the 20 most expensive SUE assets are reported in Part 6C (Boxes 788, 790, 792) of Form T661.
C. Equipment Lease Costs (Lines 350, 355 & 360 of Form T661)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are claimed as follows (buildings remain excluded except prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903):

items: Line 350 — Equipment Used ASA (≥90% of Operating Time): Under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods, 100% of lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used 90% or more of its operating time in the tax year for SR&ED in Canada is claimed on Line 350 (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method).

Line 355 — Equipment Used Primarily (>50% to <90% of Operating Time): Under the Proxy Method, 50% (half) of the lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment (other than GPOEF) used >50% to <90% of its operating time for SR&ED is claimed on Line 355 (and 0% is claimable if used ≤50% of the time, or for a lease of land). Under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters "0" on Line 355 and instead claims the exact proportional percentage of SR&ED usage for equipment used <90% of the time (or a lease of land) on Line 360 as overhead, provided the lease is directly related and incremental to SR&ED.

body.text: 4.8 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the current contract expenditure is included in the Section 37 deduction pool (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), but only 80% of the contract expenditure is included in qualified expenditures for the Section 127 ITC under Paragraph 127(9)(g). Under the look-through rule (Subsections 37(14) and 37(15)), any non-qualifying capital expenditure incurred by a contractor or subcontractor reduces the payer's eligible contract amount, and the performer must notify the payer in writing within 90 days after the end of the calendar year. Foreign SR&ED contracts are deductible under Subsection 37(2) when computing business income, but earn 0% ITC and cannot be reported on Form T661.

Where a claimant (payer) enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (Section 251), the payer's expenditure enters its Section 37 pool but does not qualify for an ITC in the payer's hands (Paragraph 127(9)(f) and Subsection 127(24)). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (unreduced by the NAL contract payment), and the NAL performer and payer may file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, Subsection 127(13)) to transfer the NAL performer's qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the payer. Finally, Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii)) made to Canadian resident corporations (Entity A, claimed when performed), approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, granting councils, or tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under Paragraph 149(1)(j) (Entities B–F, claimed when paid) for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results) are included at 100% in the Section 37 pool and 80% in Section 127 qualified expenditures, and require filing Form T1263.
4.9 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Stacking Mechanics (NRC IRAP & Provincial Credits)

Under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA (Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, updated March 27, 2026), both the Section 37 deduction pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures must be reduced on a project-by-project basis by any government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable/conditional loans, or provincial/territorial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance (Paragraph 12(1)(x)), and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date (with NAL allocations filed on Form T1145).

When stacking a direct wage grant such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (which reimburses 50% to 80% of internal R&D salaries) with federal SR&ED under the Proxy Method, the 55% PPA is calculated on the full gross SR&ED salary base before deducting the IRAP grant. For example, on $100,000 of eligible R&D wages funded by an $80,000 NRC IRAP grant, the claimant computes a $55,000 PPA (55% of $100,000), yielding $155,000 in gross qualified expenditures minus $80,000 IRAP assistance = $75,000 in net qualified expenditures (generating a $26,250 federal SR&ED refund at 35% in addition to the $80,000 IRAP grant). With respect to provincial R&D tax credits, the full provincial credit (including the portion earned on the 55% PPA) reduces Section 127 federal qualified expenditures under Subsection 127(18); however, the portion of a provincial credit attributable to the PPA does not reduce the Section 37 deduction pool and is instead included in taxable income in the year received under Paragraph 12(1)(x).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentives

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory provides a provincial or territorial R&D tax incentive that stacks with federal SR&ED. Because provincial and territorial R&D credits are government assistance under Subsection 127(9), they reduce federal qualified expenditures on Line 513 of Form T661 unless validly waived or renounced on time.

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive: Québec’s 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul and Legacy Transition

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget presented on March 25, 2025, Québec introduced the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025. The CRIC consolidates and eliminates seven legacy Québec innovation tax measures (which remain claimable only for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025): (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6); (3) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03); (4) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1); (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (6) the Industrial Design component of the Design Tax Credits (while fashion design remains eligible); and (7) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts.

Under the CRIC (claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR / RD-1029.8.CR-T, with associated group allocations on Form RD-1029.8.EN and the Québec R&D deduction on Form RD-222), any corporation with an establishment carrying on business in Québec earns a 100% refundable credit based solely on spending level rather than asset size: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 bracket. The annual Exclusion Threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec Basic Personal Amount ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026) per employee, prorated by the time each employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Crucially, in addition to standard R&D, the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec as a continuation of or in conjunction with Québec R&D (specifically regulatory testing, technological validations, and studies for initial certification/approval, product form/aesthetic/functional design, and quality control system implementation for initial certification), and includes 100% of direct salaries, 100% of capital property acquisition costs (excluding land and buildings), and 50% of Québec subcontract and university/public research centre payments. Only the R&D portion of the CRIC (Line 180 of Form RD-1029.8.CR) reduces federal SR&ED expenditures on Lines 429 and 513 of Form T661. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec updated the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE / CDAEIA — Form CO-1029.8.36.DA) to focus on e-businesses integrating artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities, including data processing and hosting while excluding maintenance and scaling.

6.2 Architecture of Form T661 (Rev. May 15, 2026) and Supplementary Schedules
Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026) is organized into ten parts:

body.text: 6.3 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Launched on April 1, 2026, the CRA's optional Pre-Claim Approval Process allows eligible businesses (CCPCs, other Canadian corporations, or partnerships operating in Canada with annual gross business income under $25 million and in good standing with the CRA) to obtain an upfront technical eligibility determination on up to 3 proposed projects (which have not been previously claimed and are not under objection/litigation). After requesting a case number on Canada.ca, the business submits Form T1322 (including a maximum 500-word uncertainty description on Line 042) and up to 10 supporting documents via My Business Account. An assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) conducts an evaluation (with a mandatory 2-to-5-hour meeting for new claimants or an optional meeting for existing claimants in good standing) and provides a written decision within 8 weeks. Pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years and cuts the CRA's processing service standard for refundable claims selected for expenditure review in half, from 180 days to 90 days.
6.4 Statutory Penalty Regimes: Claim Preparers (s. 162(5.1)) and Gross Negligence (s. 163(2))

Under Subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the ITA, Part 9 of Form T661 requires complete disclosure of every external claim preparer (name, Business Number/GST number, billing arrangement code, billing rate, and total fee paid or payable). If Part 9 information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty applies under Subsection 162(5.1), for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable (subject to a due diligence defence for the preparer under Subsection 162(5.2)), though missing Part 9 data never disallows the underlying SR&ED claim. Claimants may also file Part 9 separately on paper using the CRA's Optional Filing Measure to protect fee confidentiality.

Under Subsection 163(2) of the ITA (Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy, updated January 28, 2025), if the CRA proves on a balance of probabilities (Subsection 163(3)) that a claimant knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence made a false statement or omission on an SR&ED claim, the civil penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (Paragraph 163(2)(a), where any overstated ITC is deemed deducted first), plus (2) the entire overstated refundable ITC refund claimed (Paragraph 163(2)(d), calculated on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused any portion of the overstatement). Third-party promoters who counsel false SR&ED claims also face civil penalties under Section 163.2 (Information Circular IC01-1).
7. CRA Review Process, Audit Defence, and Leading Jurisprudence
7.1 CRA Service Standards, Joint Technical/Financial Reviews, and Dispute Resolution

The CRA's service standards for processing SR&ED claims are 60 days for claims accepted as filed, 90 days for refundable claims selected for review containing only pre-approved projects, and 180 days for all other refundable claims selected for review (while first-time claimants or those that have not claimed in 3 years may be selected for the educational First-Time Claimant Advisory Service [FTCAS]).

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), a formal review is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) across three steps: (1) First Contact, scoping the projects and issues; (2) The Review Meeting, involving interviews with the technical personnel who performed the work, a virtual or on-site facility tour, and examination of contemporaneous records (commit logs, test data, timesheets, scrap records, contracts); and (3) Review Findings, where a written Proposal Package gives the claimant 30 days to respond before a Notice of Assessment/Reassessment is issued. Claimants can escalate disputes through a three-step administrative process—(1) discussing with the RTA/FR, (2) escalating to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) / Financial Review Manager (FRM), and (3) requesting an Administrative Review for due process—followed by filing a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days of the Notice of Assessment/Reassessment and appealing to the Tax Court of Canada.
7.2 Landmark Canadian SR&ED Case Law and Audit Precedents

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520 (TCC)
Foundational judicial interpretation of "SR&ED" under ITA s. 248(1) in hydraulic physical scale modelling.

Justice Bowman established the binding Five-Question Test for SR&ED eligibility, defining "technological uncertainty" (vs. routine engineering), the 5-step hypothesis process, technological advancement (including failed hypotheses), and contemporaneous recordkeeping.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 CTC 132 (FCA)
Evidentiary standard for proving systematic investigation and repeatability of testing (Criterion 3 & Criterion 5).

The Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed Northwest Hydraulic and held that while oral testimony is admissible, taxpayers must produce affirmative documentary evidence of systematic testing and repeatable experimental results kept as the work progressed.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)
Application of the Five-Question Test to software and hardware system development.

Reaffirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic five criteria are cumulative and binding across all fields of technology; developing a new product using standard techniques known to competent specialists does not constitute SR&ED.
LGL Ltd. v. The Queen (2000 DTC 6108 FCA) & Tigney Technology Inc. v. The Queen (2000 DTC 6112 FCA)
Scope of "directly attributable" and "directly related and incremental" overhead under the Traditional Method (ITR s. 2900(2)(c)).

Confirmed that to claim overhead or administrative salaries under the Traditional Method, there must be a direct, unmediated link to the SR&ED prosecution and the cost must be strictly incremental (would not have been incurred absent the SR&ED).
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen 2011 FCA 355 (FCA)
Distinction between resolving technological uncertainty vs. routine trial-and-error troubleshooting on the shop floor.

Held that modifying machinery or moulds through standard engineering adjustments without formulating and systematically testing scientific/technological hypotheses is routine engineering, not experimental development.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen 2015 TCC 77 (TCC)
Software integration and customization vs. experimental development.

Clarified that integrating existing software frameworks or resolving compatibility bugs through standard debugging documentation does not meet the threshold of technological uncertainty unless underlying system-level limitations require new conceptual knowledge.
Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen 2016 FCA 301 (FCA)
Burden of proof on all five Northwest Hydraulic questions in mechanical product development.

The FCA upheld the disallowance of SR&ED claims where the claimant relied on empirical field trials without structured hypothesis formulation, baseline variable control, or systematic analytical records.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen 2017 TCC 6 (TCC) & Lehigh Hanson Materials Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 (TCC)
Cumulative nature of the Five-Question Test and distinction between custom engineering design and SR&ED.

Explicitly ruled that all five questions in the Northwest Hydraulic test must be answered in the affirmative; custom mechanical design using established engineering formulas—even for complex, one-of-a-kind rigging—fails Question 1 if solvable by competent professionals.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada 2021 FCA 88 (FCA)
Statutory authority of the courts vs. CRA administrative guidelines in interpreting s. 248(1) for manufacturing/tooling claims.

The FCA confirmed that it is the exclusive role of the courts to interpret the Income Tax Act, and affirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic framework properly elaborates the statutory requirement of a "systematic investigation or search".
National R&D Inc. v. Canada 2022 FCA 72 (FCA, aff'g 2020 TCC 47)
Whether the CRA's 2021 SR&ED Guidelines eliminated the requirement to follow the scientific method; admissibility of expert reports.

Landmark Ruling: (1) Even where Technological Uncertainty (Q1) is conceded in software development, failure to follow the scientific method (Q2–Q5) is fatal; (2) CRA's 2021 Guidelines did not remove the scientific method requirement; and (3) expert witness reports that opine directly on the ultimate legal question of whether work constitutes SR&ED are inadmissible.
Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. His Majesty the King 2023 TCC 35 (TCC)
Application of the Northwest Hydraulic test following Kam-Press and National R&D in materials/manufacturing processes.

Reaffirmed that notwithstanding CRA administrative guides, settled Canadian law requires strict adherence to all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, rejecting claims where testing lacked methodical hypothesis formulation and scientific rigour.

body.text: 8.2 Worked Example 2: Québec Corporation Claiming the New CRIC (30%/20%) and Federal SR&ED (Taxation Year Beginning January 1, 2026)

Consider Montréal Quantum Systems Inc., a Québec CCPC whose taxation year runs from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (beginning after March 25, 2025, and therefore governed by the Québec CRIC regime on Form RD-1029.8.CR). During 2026, the company employs 10 full-time R&D engineers in Montréal (100% dedicated to eligible R&D) earning $120,000 each ($1,200,000 total R&D wages), acquires $300,000 in new laboratory testing equipment (used 100% ASA for R&D), and pays $200,000 to an arm's-length Québec subcontractor for R&D testing.

First, under the Québec CRIC calculation, gross qualified expenditures equal $1,200,000 (100% of R&D wages) + $300,000 (100% of R&D capital equipment) + $100,000 (50% of the $200,000 Québec subcontractor payment) = $1,600,000. Second, the 2026 CRIC Exclusion Threshold is the greater of $50,000 or 10 FTE employees × $18,952 (the 2026 Québec Basic Personal Amount) = $189,520. Subtracting the $189,520 exclusion threshold from $1,600,000 leaves $1,410,480 in net excess qualified expenditures. Third, applying the two-tier CRIC rate yields 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000) plus 20% on the remaining $410,480 ($82,096), resulting in a 100% refundable Québec CRIC cash credit of $382,096.

Fourth, under the Federal SR&ED calculation (electing the Proxy Method under Bill C-15 rules), gross federal qualified expenditures equal $1,200,000 (direct wages) + $660,000 (55% PPA on $1,200,000 wages) + $160,000 (80% of the $200,000 arm's-length subcontractor) + $300,000 (new ASA capital equipment) = $2,320,000. Deducting the $382,096 Québec CRIC government assistance on Line 513 leaves $1,937,904 in net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (all within the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit), generating $678,266 in federal SR&ED ITCs at 35%. Combined, the corporation recovers $1,060,362 ($382,096 Québec CRIC + $678,266 Federal SR&ED) on $1,700,000 of total out-of-pocket R&D cash outlay—an effective 62.4% combined recovery rate.
